<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. PRO built a compelling narrative and landed real hits: the circularity of defending a seller-drafted term with the seller's drafting, and the pointed question of why decades of "license" fine print never produced a heritable tier. But CON did the more surgical work across the exchange. CON dismantled PRO's inheritable-contracts analogy (every item on the list was sold as heritable; personal contracts routinely die), showed the house analogy fails because a house can be sold and split while a non-transferable account cannot, and turned two PRO concessions into structural problems: "cannot call the button Buy" collapses the hard case into relabeling, and "opt-out buyer may pay less" collapses the easy case into CON's priced tier with a flipped default. CON also answered PRO's Q1 substantively (point-of-sale labeling never tried; DRM-free storefronts already sell heritable files) and exposed the "windfall not cost" claim as economically naive. PRO's closing reply that voiding non-transferability creates upstream bargaining pressure that disclosure lacks was a genuine answer and kept the debate competitive, but CON's closing crystallized the motion's word "guarantee" and showed PRO's rule either evaporates or becomes a compulsory bundle. CON made the decision easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.5/B5.2: CON took PRO's own A1 answer—"a storefront that cannot obtain heritable rights upstream simply cannot call the button 'Buy'"—and showed that in the hard case nothing transfers, so the "guarantee" reduces to CON's own honest-labeling remedy. Paired with B4.3's point that a maximal default plus opt-out is the least protective design for sudden deaths, this reframed PRO's concessions as CON's case under PRO's name.</best_rebuttal>
